newsitem.title: USA: Clinton could announce cabinet changes Friday.
newsitem.headline: Clinton could announce cabinet changes Friday.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday considered new faces to replace a stream of departing Cabinet members and top aides and could announce his choices at a news conference on Friday.

Leon Panetta, the White House Chief of Staff credited with restoring order to a somewhat chaotic operation, is leaving to return to California, where the former congressman is expected to run for governor.

Erskine Bowles, a North Carolina businessman and longtime Clinton friend, is reported to be a candidate to replace Panetta in the politically sensitive post. The chief of staff will have to chart a strategy for dealing with Republicans in Congress who are pressing for investigations of Clinton's campaign finances and other alleged misdeeds.
Clinton may have to fill as many as seven Cabinet posts before he is sworn in on Jan 20.

White House adviser George Stephanopoulos said on Wednesday night that Clinton would hold a news conference by the end of the week, probably on Friday. "I think you'll have that replacement (for Panetta) named very soon," Stephanopoulos said on CNN's "Larry King Live."
"It is important to have the White House structure in place early on in the transition ... to make sure we have an orderly proceess of new Cabinet announcements," he said.

Stephanopoulos, one of the president's closest advisers, also said in the CNN interview he too was likely to leave. He said he planned "to take a week to think about it on the beach" but added: "I've had a great run ... I'm probably going to move on to other things."
After a triumphant return on Wednesday and a dinner celebration with several hundred supporters, Clinton was spending Thursday discussing a new Cabinet with aides.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Defence Secretary William Perry have already told the president they will resign. Christopher was expected to hold a news conference with Clinton on Thursday to confirm his resignation, according to officials who doubted that the appointment of a successor would also be announced.

One official also said Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor was planning to return to private life and Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said she would leave. Others who may go are Transportation Secretary Federico Pena, Housing Secretary Henry Cisneros and Education Secretary Richard Riley.

Christopher, 71, and Perry, 69, had both made it known they wanted out from serving in a second term. Officials said Christopher was expected to keep his post until Clinton's inauguration while Perry may return to private life within a few months once a successor is chosen.
U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright and former Sen. George Mitchell were considered leading candidates to succeed Christopher, while CIA Director John Deutch was likely to take Perry's place.

Voters gave Clinton a partial triumph, re-electing him by a margin of 49 percent to 41 percent for Republican candidate Bob Dole but allowing the Republicans to call the shots in both houses of Congress -- a move that many predict will lead not to cooperation but to cut-throat political infighting and give-no-quarter investigations of White House scandals.
